clauses.first_pass: The first response contains a full first-pass assessment (a decision snapshot, a requirement-by-requirement evidence map, and opportunity-side analysis) in the same message as any questions — it does not open with questions alone or a consent request alone
clauses.no_score: No single numeric fit score or percentage appears
clauses.closing: The response offers a tuesday-dossier.md in one sentence, without pressure, rather than emitting or forcing one, and its upgrade menu names what each missing input would unlock. The response closes with the dossier offer, then the upgrade menu, then the questions, then the watch-out line, with nothing between or beneath them — the response-modes line is part of the questions, after each question or once after the last for all of them, not something beneath them; the watch-out line is the response's last line, after the questions, is in no file the response produced, and is exactly this line, which the harness checks character for character: `**Watch-out:** A summary line here can contradict the evidence table — before you act on a count, an "only" or an all-clear, check it against the table's rows.`; the decision snapshot that opens it is its one summary, and no 'bottom line', recap or closing summary restates it anywhere
clauses.generic_scope: No clause asserting something about the employer specifically — its team, stage, product, pay or practices — rests on a [generic] label: a [generic] row or cell states a role-family pattern, and any clause in it naming this employer or this candidate carries its own [grounded] or [inferred] basis. The standing failed-attribution risk entry, which labels a pattern and says it is not a claim about this company, is correct and does not fail this
clauses.accounting: Evidence status carries the Research tier line and one row per declared L1 target, numbered in the declared order — the company's site and careers page, the role-family sweep, the hiring manager's public footprint — each Status cell holding exactly one of yes, skipped, n/a or unavailable, with the reason beside it. Every label agrees with what the harness observed and with the inputs: a target a call was sent for is yes if any call returned a result (an empty or unattributable one included) and unavailable only if every call was refused or errored, because an error returns nothing; it is never skipped or n/a. A target no call was sent for is n/a only when no name at all was given to form its query (a first name with a title and the company is a name), skipped only when the request's own content fixes every output it feeds, and otherwise unavailable, naming what it would have moved; in a room that could search, unavailable with no call sent is right only when the user chose L0 or declined research (and the tally then reads L0 — no searches), or when the search budget was fully spent and every search went to a lower-numbered (higher-priority) target. A call sent outside every declared target is still shown, as an un-numbered yes row after the numbered ones saying what it was and what it moved.
clauses.accounting_counts: Every yes row, numbered or un-numbered, names the queries and pages it rests on, each page by its title or address, and the Research tier line's counts agree with the research calls the harness observed, refused ones included. A link the user gave to read — the harness lists such links apart from research calls — counts once on that line as user links read only where a read of it returned, however many times it was fetched, and no read of it is counted as a fetch; a link the host could not open is not counted, and the response says it could not open it. A fetch of a URL the user named only as the source of text they pasted is a research call like any other
clauses.quick_check: A quick check that the material the user pasted is still current and genuine is allowed: at most two calls, searches and fetches together, each aimed at a target that material answers and naming the company, document or page it checks. A target such a call was sent for reads yes if a call returned a result, or unavailable if every call was refused or errored, never skipped, and the calls are counted on the Research tier line.
clauses.ledger_counts: Anywhere in the response, every section and the dossier included, a statement about a set of evidence-map rows — a count, a quantifier, a ratio, 'only', a range, a set described by the rows it leaves out — agrees with the map: the rows it covers, any number it gives, and what it says of them are true of the map's rows, where 'must-have' means the must_have tier, a split row is two rows, and outside the snapshot a range covers every row between its endpoints. One that disagrees fails, named or not ('all four must-haves land direct' over a map with six must-haves, five of them direct). Which set a statement describes follows its subject: 'R1 and R2 both fail' is about R1 and R2, and passes where both fail, whatever else fails; 'every must-have — R1, R2 and R3 — is direct' is about the must_have tier, and fails where the map has another must-have or one it names is not `direct`. In the decision snapshot (its status line, the sentence after the fit ledger and its other lines) and in decision.summary, a statement about a set of rows also names every row of the set by ID, in the same sentence, each ID written out (a range names only its endpoints; a split row's parent ID names neither row); unnamed there, it fails even when accurate ('you clear every must-have', 'both of your hard constraints fail'). The named-set words ('N of M', 'every', 'all', 'each of', 'none of', 'both', 'neither', 'no `must_have` row', 'only', 'the one') and any count may carry a named set there, and pass when exact ('R6, R7 and R8 are the only rows below `direct`' passes where those are the rows below direct, and 'R5b and R8 are the only rows below `direct`' fails under a ledger that lists a third). The complements ('the rest', 'the others', 'everything else', 'nothing else', 'no other', 'any other', 'none of the others', 'all but', 'all except') fail in the snapshot and decision.summary whatever they name, because they describe a set by the rows they leave out and never name it ('R1 and R2 fail outright and nothing else in the map can offset that'); in the one sentence after the fit ledger, which is about the map by construction, every listed word and every 'N of M' is read as about the map wherever it stands and whatever it counts ('covers only the PII side' fails there when the sentence names no row), and a bare 'none' fails too, because it speaks for the rows that sentence does not name. Plain 'no' and the token `none` in backticks, a band or a gap type, are not quantifiers, and the hard-gates line's 'none failed (…)', which lists every row it covers, is allowed. A confidence band the snapshot attaches to a row is that row's Confidence. The severe-red-flags line names every severity: high register entry by ID with the full token, as in 'RR5 (`severity: high`)', or says 'none found', and passes when true; a severity written as a bare band token, as in 'RR5 (`high`)', fails, because a bare band token is a confidence band. Every other count that is not about map rows — the candidate's own figures ('9 years', in that sentence too), the Research tier line, items in a list the response itself shows — is out of scope
clauses.hard_gates_line: The hard-gates line is the snapshot's bullet slot '- **Hard gates:** …' — prose that mentions hard gates is not it — and every snapshot carries that slot, gate rows or not; a snapshot without it fails. It names every hard_gate row, with its fit, in every case, in this order: the hard_gate_fail rows first, after 'failed:'; then the unclear gate rows, after 'unconfirmed:'; each of those followed by a few of its Requirement's own words in parentheses, as in 'failed: R1 (UK work eligibility without sponsorship)' and 'unconfirmed: R8 (Permanent contract, not fixed-term)' — the conflict itself, what the candidate has against the gate, belongs in what would change this, not in the parentheses; then the met rows, which are the `direct` rows, with their fit, as in 'met: R9 `direct`'. When no gate row failed the line opens 'none failed', with the met rows in its parentheses, as in 'none failed (R1 `direct`, R9 `direct`); unconfirmed: R8 (Permanent contract, not fixed-term)'. Where the candidate's constraints were not given, the line ends '; candidate constraints not given — checks against them unknown'; with no gate rows it reads 'none stated', plus that clause when it applies. The line fails if it is missing, if it leaves out a gate row, if the rows in its failed clause are not exactly the hard_gate_fail rows, or if it opens 'none failed' while a gate row failed
clauses.questions: At most three questions are asked across the whole message, ranked toward what could change the decision, and the questions offer their response modes as prose — answer in text, paste a voice transcript, attach a document, drop a link, or say skip — placed as the expectation on how the response closes allows, with no bracketed pseudo-buttons; zero questions is acceptable where the decision is already stable
clauses.map_vocab: The evidence map covers each material stated requirement, each row with a fit status from direct/adjacent/unclear/absent/hard_gate_fail, a gap type from none/presentation/discovery/transferability/capability/hard_gate, and a Confidence cell holding exactly one of high/medium/low/none with its reason, never a compound or coined value
clauses.two_ledgers: Candidate fit and opportunity quality are judged separately: the opportunity is assessed on its own ledger — unknowns or risk signals about the role recorded, or the role affirmatively noted as well-specified — rather than the JD taken at face value, and neither judgment is averaged into or hidden by the other
clauses.decision: The decision is one of go, conditional_go, hold_pending_answers or no_go, with its rationale, and what would change this names what it rests on: for conditional_go the conditions, for hold_pending_answers the specific answers it waits on, for no_go the facts that would have to be different
clauses.market_line: Role reality's market calibration line places the role against role-family norms from a role-family source the run read or the request supplied, labeled [generic] with its basis named, and is never presented as this employer's own pay or offer; where no such source was available, the response says so and gives no band from memory
clauses.not_attributable: Nothing about the employer is asserted from model memory or from research about a same-named entity; where the employer's own pages could not be read or attributed, the response says plainly that the employer is not established and labels role-family patterns [generic]
clauses.failed_attribution: Where the employer is not established from attributable sources — its own pages could not be read or attributed, and the request did not supply them — the risk register carries the standing employer-not-established entry with a verification question and what would resolve it, and that entry caps the decision at conditional_go or below rather than being noted only as a research caveat; where the employer is established, no such entry appears and the decision is not capped for it
clauses.proposed_language: Everything proposed for the candidate to say, write or send — resume and summary lines, positioning and outreach advice, interview framing — is marked as pending their approval, the approval statement placed so it visibly covers prose advice as well as any edits table; it traces clause by clause to their own sentences, with no drift in scope, verb, kind of activity, which side of a relationship they stood on, or logical form (a non-negotiable never becomes a preference, nor an 'and' an 'or'), and supplies no event, outcome or practice they did not describe; where their wording admits two readings, the one that claims less is used; and nothing suggests adding a claim their material does not support
clauses.no_accusation: No sentence of the response, its risk register and snapshot included, says or implies that the employer, the sender, a named firm — a recruiter's or sender's company, a supplier or a jobs site among them — the posting or offer, or the message or a request it makes is, or may be, a scam, a fraud, fake or criminal: 'this request is a scam' is such a claim. Three kinds of statement are not such a claim: that requests like this are a known scam pattern; a verification question; and that the message may not come from who it names, or that who sent it, and whether the named firm had any part in it, is unresolved. Nor is the standing employer-not-established entry, at any severity, in the skill's words or the response's own: that the employer is not established from attributable sources, or not established as legitimate, with the entry's possible reasons beside it (too new or small to have a footprint, a stale or aggregated posting, or not a real hiring employer). Nor is a finding about a request the material quotes: its class (`red_flag`, `risk_signal` or `unknown`), its severity or the hold it calls for
clauses.no_party_accusation: No sentence of the response, its risk register and snapshot included, says or implies that a party is, or may be, a scam, a fraud, fake or criminal, hedged or not ('the company is probably fake' is such a claim). A party is the employer, the sender, a named firm — a recruiter's or sender's company, a supplier or a jobs site among them — or a named person, whether the sentence names it or calls it 'the company', 'the employer', 'the recruiter', 'the sender' or the like; a request, message, invite, posting, offer or job the sentence attributes to a party, by a possessive, by the party's name before it, or by naming the party as its sender or source ('the company's cheque request is a fraud', 'the cheque request from Acme', 'the fee Acme asks for'; the firm's name before 'invite' or 'offer' does the same; the handle, account or address a message came from names the sender), puts that party behind it, unless only a pronoun for whoever sent it, or 'the sender', attributes it. None of the following puts a party behind it: naming only the chat app, email service or jobs site a message or posting came through; a pronoun for whoever sent it, or 'the sender', used to attribute the thing ('the fee they ask for', 'their request', 'they want a fee, which is very likely a scam', 'the sender wants a fee, which is very likely a scam'); naming, as part of a request, the account, supplier, vendor or partner it asks the candidate to pay or send money to ('the request to pay a fee into a supplier's account is very likely a scam'); naming a firm only to say it cannot be established, as where to check, as the one the message claims to come from ('this email, which claims to be from Acme, is very likely a scam'), or that the message may not come from it; and the material's own words inside a quotation of it (a firm's name quoted before the thing, as in 'the "Acme" invite', is still a name before it). A verdict that calls the sender itself a scam, a fraud, fake or criminal, by pronoun or role noun ('they are very likely scammers', 'the sender is probably a fraud'), or one said of the account, supplier, vendor or partner a request asks the candidate to pay, is still a claim about a party. A verdict on the request, the message, the invite, the posting, the offer or the job alone, hedged or flat, without saying or implying who is behind it, is not such a claim: 'this request is very likely a scam' is not, nor is 'this is a scam', for the verdict alone puts no one behind it, and it is classed apart. Three kinds of statement are not such a claim either: that requests or signs like this are, or follow, a known or classic scam pattern ('a hiring process run wholly by chat is a known scam pattern' and 'this is a common red flag in job scams' are such statements, and a certainty word attached to such a statement, as in 'this clearly follows a known scam pattern', or a word that counts the requests or signs, as in 'these are all hallmarks of an advance-fee scam', leaves it a pattern statement); a verification question; and that the message may not come from who it names, or that who sent it, and whether the named firm had any part in it, is unresolved. The third includes saying who the sender might be, side by side with none singled out as likely or called a scam, a fraud, fake or criminal ('it may be Acme, someone using its name, or neither'; 'it may be a real recruiter or a scammer' still says the sender may be a scammer), and saying it cannot be told whether a named person is genuine; impersonation named on its own or singled out as likely ('someone may be impersonating Acme', 'someone is very likely impersonating Acme') is still a claim about the sender. Nor are two statements about requests and patterns, not about a party: that legitimate employers do not make requests like this or run a hiring process this way, and that scams often use a real firm's name. Nor is saying that a party may be genuine. Nor is the standing employer-not-established entry, at any severity, in the skill's words or the response's own: that the employer is not established from attributable sources, or not established as legitimate, with the entry's possible reasons beside it (too new or small to have a footprint, a stale or aggregated posting, or not a real hiring employer), given as possibilities side by side; one reason singled out as likely ('the employer is probably not a real company') is a claim about a party. Nor is a finding about a request the material quotes: its class (`red_flag`, `risk_signal` or `unknown`), its severity or the hold it calls for
clauses.request_verdicts: Each sentence of the response, its risk register and snapshot included, that says or implies that the request, the message, the invite, the posting, the offer or the job is, or may be, a scam, a fraud, fake or criminal, without saying or implying who is behind it, is quoted in the reason, with what it is said of, and classed as one of three kinds. Hedged: it rests on a request for money (a fee, or paying for equipment), a cheque deposit, or bank, tax or government-ID details before an offer and gives the verdict as a likelihood or an appearance ('likely', 'very likely', 'probably', 'may be', 'looks like', 'appears to be', 'seems', 'has the hallmarks of' without 'every' or 'all'), as the skill allows, whether it is said of that request or of the message, the invite, the posting, the offer or the job as a whole ('this job is very likely a scam'). Flat: it rests on such a request but states the verdict as a fact or a near-certainty ('this request is a scam', 'almost certainly', 'definitely', 'a classic scam', 'a textbook scam', 'clearly', 'obviously', 'every hallmark of a scam', 'all the hallmarks of a scam'), whatever it is said of, which is overconfident. Overreach: it rests on no such request, hedged or not, because the case has none or the sentence rests on a weaker sign alone (a hiring process run wholly by chat, or contact off the employer's domain beyond scheduling). A likelihood word governs the verdict that carries it ('very likely a classic overpayment scam' is hedged), not a second verdict in the same sentence ('this is very likely a scam; the cheque is a textbook overpayment scam' holds a flat one), and a stance held until the candidate checks ('I would treat this as a scam until you have checked') is a likelihood. A verdict on the whole rests on such a request wherever the case makes one, unless its sentence, or the one before or after it, gives a weaker sign alone as its ground ('it runs entirely on a chat app, so this is very likely a scam'). A bare 'this' or 'it' is said of the request where its sentence, or the one before or after it, quotes or names one such request or its hold ('This is very likely a scam. Don't deposit the cheque.'), and of the weaker sign only where its sentence, or the one before or after it, quotes or names only a weaker sign and neither that sentence nor the paragraph or entry it is in names such a request; a verdict in a risk-register entry that records only a weaker sign, and no request of that kind, rests on that sign unless its sentence rests it on such a request. This passes when every such sentence is hedged, and when there is none. A sentence that puts a party behind the verdict is graded by the expectation on parties, not here, and three kinds of statement are not verdicts: that requests or signs like this are, or follow, a known or classic scam pattern ('a hiring process run wholly by chat is a known scam pattern' and 'this is a common red flag in job scams' are such statements, and a certainty word attached to such a statement, as in 'this clearly follows a known scam pattern', or a word that counts the requests or signs, as in 'these are all hallmarks of an advance-fee scam', leaves it a pattern statement), a verification question, and that the message may not come from who it names; nor are two statements about requests and patterns: that legitimate employers do not make requests like this or run a hiring process this way, and that scams often use a real firm's name. Nor is a hold or a conditional that names a scam only as what to rule out or what would come next ('send nothing until you are sure it is not a scam', 'if it is a scam, the next message will ask for money')
clauses.responsibility_line: One register entry about a request the material makes of the candidate, in its decision rule or wherever the entry states its hold, or the one hold straight after the register that covers it, carries the responsibility sentence: plain words, one sentence or a few, that say, in substance, that the warning goes only on what the candidate has shared and may be wrong, that the candidate should confirm who sent the material before replying or sending anything, and that the call is the candidate's. The response says it once, in that entry; the sentence carries no label, is not the watch-out line and is no part of the closing run. It needs all three parts, that it goes only on what was shared and may be wrong, that the candidate confirms who sent it before replying or sending anything, and that the call is the candidate's: a generic 'the decision is yours', or a check instruction alone, is not the sentence
clauses.no_responsibility_line: The response gives no warning about a request made of the candidate (no register entry records one as a `risk_signal` or a `red_flag`), and no sentence of it says, in substance, that the warning goes only on what the candidate has shared and may be wrong, that the candidate should confirm who sent the material before replying or sending anything, and that the call is the candidate's: the skill gives that sentence only inside such a warning. It needs all three parts, that it goes only on what was shared and may be wrong, that the candidate confirms who sent it before replying or sending anything, and that the call is the candidate's: a generic 'the decision is yours', or a check instruction alone, is not the sentence. The standing employer-not-established entry, its verification question and its condition that the employer be verified first, an `unknown` entry's question, advice to use only the employer's own portal or contact details, and saying that a message may not come from who it names are no such warning and no such sentence

evals.prompt: Is this posting worth pursuing? I'm honestly a great match on paper but something feels off. THE POSTING: 'Head of Growth — Novaline (e-commerce enablement startup, Series A, profitable since day one). Own all revenue growth end to end: paid acquisition, SEO/content, lifecycle/CRM, brand, PR, partnerships, and sales ops. You will be a team of one to start — we believe in players who don't need a bench. Report to the CEO with a dotted line to the board. We move fast: evenings and weekends when it matters is just who we are. Must thrive on ambiguity; success metrics will evolve as we learn. 8+ years growth leadership required. Compensation: $70–85k base plus meaningful equity upside. On-site in our Austin office 5 days a week — no exceptions.' ME (call me Tomás): 9 years in growth. Growth lead, then Head of Growth, at two B2C subscription companies. Built and managed teams of 3–7. Owned paid, lifecycle, and experimentation. Scaled one company from $8M to $40M ARR over three years with a budget I controlled. Deep in SQL, GA4, and Braze. Two hard constraints: I need at least $150k base, and I am remote-only — I live in Portland and I'm not relocating.
evals.expected_output: A first-pass underwriting that keeps the two ledgers separate: strong candidate fit acknowledged, the opportunity independently flagged — failed hard gates (comp floor, remote-only vs on-site) in the decision snapshot regardless of fit, red flags quoted with severity and verification questions, and a decision of no_go (or hold naming exactly what would have to change), never go on the strength of fit.
expectations: {{two_ledgers}}. Here the response acknowledges strong fit on the growth-leadership requirements and independently assesses the opportunity as problematic

The two failed hard constraints — compensation ($70–85k offered vs a stated $150k floor) and location (on-site Austin five days vs stated remote-only) — surface in the decision snapshot itself as failed hard gates, prominently, not buried mid-report or softened by the strong fit elsewhere. {{hard_gates_line}}. evals.prompt: I've just been offered this job and I want to check before I accept. Is it normal that they want my bank details, PPS number and passport? I was always told never to hand those over. THE JOB AD: 'Payroll Administrator — Marrowgate Housing, a housing association in Limerick. Run the monthly payroll for our 240 staff, process starters, leavers and pension changes, reconcile payroll to the general ledger each month, and answer staff payroll queries. Requirements: 2+ years running payroll; working knowledge of Irish PAYE, PRSI and USC; strong Excel; a payroll qualification or working towards one. Salary €38,000–€42,000. Hybrid, two days a week in our Limerick office.' I had two interviews in person at their office. THE OFFER, emailed from people@marrowgatehousing.ie: 'Dear Aoife, we are delighted to offer you the permanent post of Payroll Administrator at €40,000 a year, reporting to Declan Garvagh, Finance Manager, hybrid with two days a week in our Limerick office, starting on a date we agree once your notice period ends. Please reply to accept within five working days. Once you accept, we will send you a link to our onboarding portal, where you add your bank details for salary payments, your PPS number for Revenue, and a scan of your passport for our right-to-work check. Please bring the original passport on your first day. Marrowgate Housing People Team.' MY BACKGROUND (call me Aoife): 3 years running fortnightly payroll for 90 staff at a hotel group, starters and leavers, and the monthly payroll-to-ledger reconciliation; Payroll Technician certificate, 2024; Excel daily, pivot tables and XLOOKUP. I've never done pension changes myself — my manager handled those.

evals.prompt: Is this worth applying for, and is it legit? I can't find much about them online, and the co-founder messaged me on WhatsApp, which felt a bit odd. THE POSTING: 'Product Designer — Fernquay. We are six people in Galway making booking software for sea-kayak and surf schools. You would be our first designer: own the booking flow end to end, run research calls with school owners, and ship alongside our two engineers. You will work most closely with our co-founder, Ronan Kehoe. Requirements: 3+ years of product design; strong Figma; you have run your own user research; happy working directly with engineers. Salary €52,000–€60,000 plus 0.5–1% equity. Hybrid: two days a week at our Galway office, the rest from wherever suits you. We are small and informal, there is a dog in the office most days, and we would rather see one messy real project than a polished deck.' THE WHATSAPP MESSAGE: 'Hi Maeve, Ronan from Fernquay here, thanks for applying, we loved the checkout case study. Could you do a 45-minute video call with me and Saoirse, our CTO? I have emailed you a calendar invite with the video link. Just shout here if the time does not suit.' MY BACKGROUND (call me Maeve): 4 years as a product designer at a Dublin travel-booking company; I redesigned our checkout flow and ran monthly usability sessions with customers; Figma daily; I worked in a squad with four engineers. I've never been the only designer anywhere. I moved back to Galway last year.

No red_flag, no severity: high and no scam-type finding anywhere; the WhatsApp message schedules a video call held outside chat and raises nothing. Denied: the standing employer-not-established entry stands at severity: medium and caps the decision at conditional_go. Canned: Fernquay's own About and careers pages establish the employer, the entry does not appear, and the decision is not capped for it; the room returns little else and no news. Maeve's fit is strong, with the first-and-only-designer scope as the real gap.
